analysis.one_liner: Changes the health care law so employers only owe insurance to workers averaging 40 hours a week instead of 30.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 248-179 in April 2014, but the Senate never voted, so the 30-hour rule stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act required larger employers to offer health insurance to employees working at least 30 hours a week or face penalties. This bill raised that threshold to 40 hours, which would exempt many workers who put in 30 to 39 hours a week from any employer obligation to cover them. The bill cleared the House in April 2014 but the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Larger employers gain the most: under the 40-hour definition, they no longer owe coverage or risk penalties for the many workers who put in 30 to 39 hours a week, and it becomes cheaper to keep those employees' hours under 40. Workers who need health coverage but cannot get full-time hours gain nothing and could lose the offer of coverage they would have had under the 30-hour rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Larger employers with many hourly workers

how_it_helps.text: Redefines a full-time employee for the ACA employer mandate from 30 to 40 hours a week, so employers owe coverage or penalties for far fewer workers.
Applies to months beginning after December 31, 2013, meaning employers could stop counting 30-39 hour workers toward the mandate almost immediately.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on workers clocking 30-39 hours a week, who would be easiest to keep below the coverage threshold, and on the Affordable Care Act's employer-coverage requirement overall, which becomes harder to enforce.

drawbacks.text: Raising the full-time threshold from 30 to 40 hours means employers no longer owe coverage to employees working 30-39 hours a week, so some workers could have hours cut or lose access to employer health insurance.
Because fewer employees count as full-time for the employer mandate, the bill weakens the Affordable Care Act's requirement that larger employers provide health coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers gain flexibility and avoid penalty exposure; the cost falls on workers who would have qualified for employer coverage under the 30-hour definition and on the ACA's coverage framework generally. The bill offers nothing in return for the coverage some workers would lose.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 248-179, but the Senate put it on its calendar and never voted, and the Congress ended in January 2015 with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 248-179 on April 3, 2014, with 230 of 232 Republicans in favor and 18 of 199 Democrats.

A Democratic motion to add protections — barring the bill from taking effect if any worker lost coverage or wages, if the deficit rose, or if premiums, pre-existing condition coverage, or women's access to care were harmed — failed 191-232, with all Republicans voting no.
The bill was received in the Senate on April 7, 2014, read twice, and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, but no further action was taken.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still on the Senate calendar, so it died without a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have gained flexibility under a 40-hour definition avoided the change, and the ACA's 30-hour employer coverage requirement stayed in place; workers at risk of losing offers of coverage were spared, while the bill itself never reached the President.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; and workers spared coverage loss

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the House.

for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the House on a party-line 23-14 vote.

for.name: 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage 248-179 on April 3, 2014.

against.name: Senate Democrats (no floor action)
against.role: Senate majority party in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was nearly straight party: 230 of 232 Republicans voted yes and 179 of 199 Democrats voted no, with 18 Democrats crossing over.

industries.note: The bill sharply reduces how many workers count as full-time under the employer mandate, cutting both the risk of penalties and the number of workers employers must offer coverage. Fewer workers qualify, so some could see hours trimmed or lose the offer of employer insurance.
Employer coverage is the core of insurer revenue; reducing the employer mandate could shift some workers toward ACA marketplaces instead. The net effect on the industry is genuinely two-sided.
